region.en: Cairn Feargall, Co. Westmeath, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭西米斯郡費加爾石冢（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish vision-tale tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. IV, eBook #14465

summary.en: A giant with a squealing pig in an iron fork, a girl shoving him on, a man with twelve eyes, an armour-proof ram, and a hag whose grey gown withers men — Finn's five find themselves at a hostelry where the wells give honey-then-gall and bitter healing. When he wakes it is all explained by Cuanna of Innistuil: the giant is Sluggishness pushed by Liveliness, the twelve-eyed man the World, the ram the Desires of Men, the hag Old Age, and the two wells Lying and Truth.
summary.zh: 持鐵叉插尖嘯肥豬的巨人、推他前行的少女、十二眼老人、刀劍不入的公羊、灰袍能使青年衰老的老嫗——芬恩五人宿於一處奇異客邸：兩井之水一甜後苦、一苦而癒。醒來庫安納解釋一切：巨人即怠惰、少女即勤快、十二眼者即世界、公羊即人慾、老嫗即暮年、二井即謊言與真理。

sensitivity.note: A didactic vision-tale (aislinge) grafted onto the Fenian cycle; the allegorical bestiary and twin wells parallel didactic literature across traditions. Coordinates symbolic at the cairn where the vision began.

passages.text: It happened one day Finn and Oisin and Caoilte and Diarmuid and Lugaidh's Son went up on the top of Cairn Feargall, and their five hounds with them. They saw a giant coming towards them, very tall and rough, having an iron fork on his back and a squealing pig between the prongs of the fork, and a beautiful eager young girl behind the giant, shoving him on before her. Before they came to them, a dark Druid mist rose up that hid the road, and when it cleared away they saw a good light-roofed house at the edge of a ford, and before it two wells, on the edge of one a rough iron vessel, on the edge of the other a copper vessel. In the house was a very old white-haired man at the door, the beautiful young girl near him, the great rough giant boiling a pig by the fire, and on the other side an old countryman having dark-grey hair and twelve eyes in his head, and there was a ram in the house with a white belly and a very black head, and dark-blue horns and green feet.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: Caoilte brought Finn a drink from the copper vessel, and there was the taste of honey on it while he was drinking and the taste of gall after, so that fierce windy pains and signs of death came on him; and the drink out of the iron vessel was bitter as any battle, but no sooner did he drink it than his own colour and appearance came back to him. The ram seized the quarter of the pig set before the Fianna, and no sword could harm him, for they slipped from his back as from a rock — until the man with the twelve eyes took him by the feet and threw him out from the door. And the hag rose up and threw her pale grey gown over Finn's four comrades, and they turned to four old men, weak and withered; but Finn slept with his head in the man's breast, and the hag took her covering off the four men, and when Finn awoke they were in their own shape again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: "As to the giant you saw first, having the squealing pig in the prongs of his fork, Sluggishness is his name; and the girl shoving him along is Liveliness, for liveliness goes farther in the winking of an eye than the foot can travel in a year. The old man with the twelve bright eyes betokens the World; the ram betokens the Desires of Men; the hag is Old Age, and her gown withered up your four comrades. And the two wells betoken Lying and Truth, for it is sweet to people to be telling a lie, but it is bitter in the end. Cuanna from Innistuil is my name, and I took a very great love for you because of your wisdom, and so I put these things in your way that I might see you. And the hospitality of Cuanna's house to Finn will be the name of this story to the end of the world." And when they awoke in the morning, it is where they were, on the top of Cairn Feargall, and their dogs and their arms beside them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. IV; not verbatim.

title.en: The Banners and Named Swords of the Fianna

region.en: Magh Leine, Co. Westmeath, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭西米斯郡瑪格·萊恩（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. V, eBook #14465

summary.en: Nine of the Fianna hunting for a pup meet the three armies of the sons of the King of Ruadhleath — Cat-Heads, Dog-Heads, and White-Backs — and destroy them all. In the same telling the cycle assembles its iconography: Finn's banner the Sun-Shape, Oisin's the Dark Deadly One, Conan's a briar; the named swords won from Lon son of Liobhan, a one-footed, one-eyed smith with seven-handed brothers; and Finn's shield that calls out and is heard through all Ireland.
summary.zh: 九名菲亞納為尋一幼犬，遭遇魯拉德王三軍——貓首、犬首、白背——盡數殲滅。同一敘事中並羅列菲亞納圖騰：芬恩之「日形」旗、歐辛之「暗冥」旗、科南之荊棘旗；眾人自獨足獨眼的鐵匠隆之子處贏得名劍；以及一鳴即可傳遍全愛爾蘭的風暴盾。

sensitivity.note: Marvel-races (Cat-Heads, Dog-Heads, White-Backs) are voyage-literature stereotypes; the banner-and-weapon inventory is heraldic charter material of the cycle, best classed as a place/object-myth. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: Nine of the Fianna set out one time looking for a pup they wanted, and they searched through many places before they found it. While they were going from place to place, they saw the three armies of the sons of the King of Ruadhleath coming towards them: cat-headed one army was, and the one alongside of it was dog-headed, and the men of the third army were white-backed. When the Fianna saw them coming, Finn held up his shining spear, and light-hearted Caoilte gave out a great shout that was heard in Almhuin, and in Magh Leine, and in Teamhair, and in Dun Reithlein, and that shout was answered by Goll, son of Morna, and by Faolan, Finn's son that was with him, and by the Stutterers from Burren, and by Cael of the Sharp Sword, that never gave his ear to tale-bearers.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: It is pleasant the sound was then of the spears and the armies and of the silken banners raised up in the gusty wind of the morning. Finn's banner, the Dealb-Greine, the Sun-Shape, had the likeness of the sun on it; Oisin's banner was the Donn Nimhe, the Dark Deadly One; Caoilte's was the Lamh Dearg, the Red Hand; and merry Diarmuid's banner was the Liath Loinneach, the Shining Grey; and as to Conan, it is a briar he had on his banner, because he was always for quarrels and for trouble — it used to be said of him he never saw a man frown without striking him, or a door left open without going in through it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the Fianna had raised their banners they attacked the three armies, and first of all they killed the whole of the Cat-Heads, and then they took the Dog-Heads in hand and made an end of them, and of the White-Backs along with them. And some of the Fianna had swords that had names to them, Mac an Luin, Son of the Waves, that belonged to Finn; and Ceard-nan Gallan, the Smith of the Branches, that was Oisin's; and Caoilte's Cruadh-Chosgarach, the Hard Destroying One. They got those swords from Lon, son of Liobhan, one of the three smiths of the King of Lochlann, a young man very big and ugly, having but one foot and one eye and a blunt ploughshare turning to red in his hand; they followed him all through Ireland to his smithy, where four smiths with seven hands each were working, and the swords were made before their eyes.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. V; not verbatim.

title.en: Finn's Shield Made from Balor's Hazels

region.en: Site of Magh Tuireadh, Co. Sligo, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭斯利戈郡莫伊蒂拉戰場（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian cycle linking to the Mythological cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. V, eBook #14465

summary.en: After Lugh struck the head off Balor of the Evil Eye he hung it in the fork of a hazel-tree, which split and shed its leaves under the dripping poison and became for fifty years a dwelling of crows and ravens. When Manannan passing by had it dug up, a mist of poison rose from the roots and killed two nines of his men and blinded the third; and of the wood Luchtaine the Carpenter made a shield for Manannan, that passed to Tadg son of Nuada and so to his grandson Finn, and when Finn's shield called out it could be heard all through Ireland.
summary.zh: 盧格斬下邪眼巴洛之首懸於榛樹杈間，樹身劇裂、葉落於毒滴之下，五十年間為鴉群棲所。瑪那南命人掘樹，根間毒霧升起，兩個九人先後斃命，第三個九人雙目皆盲。木匠魯克坦以樹木為瑪那南製盾；後傳至努阿達之子塔格，再傳其孫芬恩——芬恩之盾一鳴，全愛爾蘭皆聞。

sensitivity.note: This shield-genealogy welds the Fenian cycle to the Second Battle of Magh Tuireadh — the poisoned head and withered hazel parallel the story of Lug's head among the Ulster tales. Object biography from god to mortal hero is a relic-transit motif.

passages.text: At the time of the Great Battle of Magh Tuireadh, Lugh, after he had struck the head off Balor of the Evil Eye, hung it in the fork of a hazel-tree. And the tree split, and the leaves fell from it with the dint of the poison that dropped from the head. And through the length of fifty years that tree was a dwelling-place of crows and of ravens.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: And at the end of that time Manannan, son of Lir, was passing by, and he took notice of the tree that it was split and withered, and he bade his men to dig it up. And when they began to dig, a mist of poison rose up from the roots, and nine of the men got their death from it, and another nine after them, and the third nine were blinded. And Luchtaine the Carpenter made a shield of the wood of that hazel for Manannan. And after a while Manannan gave it, and a set of chessmen along with it, to Tadg, son of Nuada; and from him it came to his grandson, Finn, son of Muirne and of Cumhal. And besides his sword, Mac an Luin, Finn had a shield that was called Sgiath Gailbhinn, the Storm Shield; and when it called out it could be heard all through Ireland.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. V; not verbatim.

region.en: Tethra, Luigne of Midhe, Co. Meath, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭米斯郡盧伊涅·梅德地區

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. VI, eBook #14465

summary.en: Lomna the fool of Finn's household sees Coirpre going secretly to Finn's wife and, too faithful to tell, writes the treachery in an ogham riddle on a four-square rod. Finn reads it; the wronged woman has the fool's head struck off and carried to Coirpre's feast, where the head, cheated of its share of fish against the law of the Fianna, speaks a prophecy — and Finn, following his hounds and his divination of rhymes, comes in and makes an end of Coirpre and his men.
summary.zh: 芬恩家中弄臣洛姆納撞見科爾普雷私通芬恩之妻，忠而不言，遂以四方形榛杖上的歐甘謎語記下此樁背叛。芬恩解讀後，被羞辱的婦人命人斬下弄臣之首送往科爾普雷宴席；眾人分魚獨缺其份——違反菲亞納之法——首級遂開口預言。芬恩循獵犬與詩謎占卜而至，誅科爾普雷及其黨羽。

sensitivity.note: The speaking head is a classic Celtic head-cult motif (cf. Bran's head); divination by rhymes (imbas forosnai form) is attested practice in the tradition. The ogham riddle on the rod is legal-poetic shorthand. Pin symbolic in Luigne.

passages.text: Finn took a wife one time of the Luigne of Midhe, and at the same time there was in his household one Lomna, a fool. Finn went into Tethra hunting with the Fianna, but Lomna stopped at the house, and after a while he saw Coirpre, a man of the Luigne, go in secretly to where Finn's wife was. The woman begged and prayed of Lomna to hide it from Finn, and Lomna agreed to that, but it preyed on him to have a hand in doing treachery on Finn. After a while he took a four-square rod and wrote an Ogham on it, and these were the words he wrote: "An alder stake in a paling of silver; deadly night-shade in a bunch of cresses; a husband of a lewd woman; a fool among the well-taught Fianna; heather on bare Ualann of Luigne."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VI; not verbatim.

passages.text: Finn saw the message, and there was anger on him against the woman; and she knew well it was from Lomna he had heard the story, and she sent a message to Coirpre bidding him come and kill the fool. So Coirpre came and struck his head off, and brought it away with him. When Finn came back in the evening he saw the body without a head, and did the divination of rhymes: "It is the body of Lomna; it is not by a wild boar he was killed; it is by his enemies he died." They let out the hounds on the track of Coirpre, and came to a house where he was cooking fish on a spit, and Lomna's head on a spike beside the fire.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VI; not verbatim.

passages.text: Coirpre divided the fish between his men, but put no bit into the mouth of the head, and that was against the law of the Fianna; and the head spoke: "A speckled white-bellied salmon that grows from a small fish under the sea; you have shared a share that is not right; the Fianna will avenge it upon you, Coirpre." "Put the head outside," said Coirpre, "for that is an evil word for us." Then the head said from outside: "It is in many pieces you will be; it is great fires will be lighted by Finn in Luigne." And as it said that, Finn came in, and he made an end of Coirpre, and of his men.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VI; not verbatim.

title.en: The Bird of Iron Beak and the War of Ilbrec and Lir
title.zh: 鐵喙之鳥與伊爾布雷克、利爾之戰

region.en: Sidhe of Ess Ruadh, Co. Sligo, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭斯利戈郡埃斯·魯阿仙丘

texts.period: Fenian-Sidhe interface tradition, medieval Irish; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. VII, eBook #14465

summary.en: A bird with an iron beak and a tail of fire comes every evening to a golden window of Ilbrec's house in the hill of Ess Ruadh and shakes itself till weapons fall on the heads of the household, and nothing thrown at it will touch it — the doing of Lir of Sidhe Fionnachaidh, with whom Ilbrec is at war. Caoilte casts it down with a copper rod, and next day meets Lir himself hand to hand: the oldest of the Men of Dea falls by the Fianna's best runner, and Derg breaks two backs with one cast of his spear.
summary.zh: 每晚一隻鐵喙火尾之鳥飛至埃斯·魯阿仙丘伊爾布雷克家中的金窗，抖落神威，使兵器紛紛砸向家僕頭頂；擲物擊之而毫髮無傷——此乃與伊爾布雷克交戰的西德·菲奧納凱德之王利爾所為。卡爾特擲銅杖將其擊落；次日與利爾親手相搏——神族中最年長者竟亡於菲亞納最快跑者之手；德格一矛貫穿二人後背。

sensitivity.note: The ruinous bird is the fixed Fenian marvel (compare the geilt bird of Suibhne lore); a feud among two Sidhe-kings witnessed and settled by a mortal champion is a good instance of the mortal-arbiter motif. Pin is the documented hill.

passages.text: One time Caoilte was hunting on Beinn Gulbain, and he went on to Ess Ruadh, and when he came near the hill of the Sidhe that is there, he saw a young man waiting for him, Derg, son of Eoghan of the people of Usnach, his foster-brother, now living among his mother's people the Tuatha de Danaan. "There is nothing wanting to us there of food or of clothing," said the young man, "but for all that I would sooner live the life of the worst treated of the serving-boys of the Fianna than the life I am living in the hill of the Sidhe." And he brought Caoilte into the hill.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: At that time there was great war between Lir of Sidhe Fionnachaidh and Ilbrec of Ess Ruadh. There used a bird with an iron beak and a tail of fire to come every evening to a golden window of Ilbrec's house, and there he would shake himself till he would not leave sword on pillow, or shield on peg, or spear in rack, but they would come down on the heads of the people of the house; and whatever they would throw at the bird, it is on the heads of some of themselves it would fall.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Caoilte put his hand within the rim of his shield and took out a copper rod, and made a cast of it at the bird that brought it down on the floor of the hall. Ilbrec took down a sharp spear having thirty rivets of gold in it and gave it to Caoilte: "That is the Spear of Fiacha, son of Congha, and it is with that Finn made an end of Aillen, son of Midhna, that used to burn Teamhair." In the morning three brave armies of Lir came all about the hill, and the host of the Sidhe went out to the battle, and the fight went on from the rising of the day till midday.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: And then Caoilte and Lir met with one another, and they made a very fierce fight, and at the last Lir of Sidhe Fionnachaidh fell by the hand of Caoilte. Then the two good champions Dubh and Donn, sons of Eirrge, fought on, Dubh in the front of the whole army and Donn behind all, guarding the rear; but Derg put his finger into the thong of his spear and made a cast at the one that was nearest him, and it broke his back and went on into the body of the other, so that the one cast made an end of the two; and that ended the battle, and all that was left of the great army of Lir went wearing away to the north.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: Caoilte's Healing and the Drink of Remembrance
title.zh: 卡爾特療傷與記憶之飲

region.en: Hill of the Sidhe at Ess Ruadh, Co. Sligo, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭斯利戈郡埃斯·魯阿仙丘

texts.period: Fenian-Sidhe interface tradition, medieval Irish; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. VII, eBook #14465

summary.en: Poisoned in the thigh by a spear of Mane son of the King of Lochlann, Caoilte rides to Ess Ruadh for Bebind, daughter of Elcmar, keeper of what is left of Goibniu's ale and the Tuatha de Danaan's drink of healing. First the household must be freed of its yearly terrors: Cascorach the musician slays the visiting woman-warrior of Lochlann, Caoilte strikes down the King of Lochlann with the spear called War-Woman, and the three death-screeching ravens that carry off hurling boys are killed with chessmen for casts. Then comes the five-drink cure, the washing of Flann daughter of Flidais, and the parting gifts — the fish-hook that takes fish in any water, and the drink of remembrance that keeps every battle in memory for ever.
summary.zh: 洛赫蘭王之子的毒矛傷了卡爾特大腿，他奔赴埃斯·魯阿，求助於保有哥伊布努殘酒與神族療傷水的艾爾克瑪爾之女貝賓德。先解除仙丘的年 年之災：樂師卡斯卡拉赫誅殺來犯女戰士；卡爾特擲「戰女矛」擊斃洛赫蘭王；三隻叼走擲球少年之烏鴉被以棋子擊殺。而後行五飲之治、弗蕾丹之女弗蘭的洗頭之術；臨別贈禮——無水不獲魚的魚鉤，以及令百戰永誌不忘的記憶之飲。

sensitivity.note: The drink of remembrance is the narrative device that licenses the aged Caoilte's testimony to St Patrick — a metanarrative function of Fenian tales; wound-suction healing and the five-drink cure parallel the Conn Crither well of healing. Tag 'prophetic-vision' omitted in favour of resurrection+voyage.

passages.text: It was in a battle at Beinn Edair in the east that Mane, son of the King of Lochlann, made a cast at Caoilte in the middle of the battle with a deadly spear; it struck into his thigh, and left its poison in it, so that he had to go in search of healing. And it is where he went, to the hill of the Sidhe at Ess Ruadh, to ask help of Bebind, daughter of Elcmar of Brugh na Boinne, that had the drink of healing of the Tuatha de Danaan, and all that was left of the ale of Goibniu.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Caoilte called to Cascorach the Musician, son of Caincenn, and bade him bring his harp and come along with him; and there was a woman-warrior used to come every year with the ships of the men of Lochlann to make an attack on the Tuatha de Danaan, and there was no precious thing in all the hills of the Sidhe but she had knowledge of it, and would bring it away. It was Cascorach went out against her, and she used high words when she saw so young a man coming to fight with her, but he made an end of her for all her high talk, and left her lying on the strand with the sea foam washing up to her.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: As to Caoilte, he went out in a chariot belonging to Midhir of the Yellow Hair, and a spear was given him that was called Ben-badb, the War-Woman, and he made a cast of it that struck the King of Lochlann, that he fell in the middle of his army, and the life went from him. And there came three flocks of beautiful red birds from Slieve Fuad eating the green grass before the hill, and Caoilte and his comrades drove them away with stones; and there were three ravens come to them every year out of the north, and the time the young lads of the hill are playing their hurling, each one of the ravens carries off a boy of them. On the morrow the whole of the Tuatha de Danaan went out to look at the hurling, and the three ravens from the north came over the sea and pitched on the great tree of power, and gave three gloomy screeches that took the courage out of the whole gathering; and Cascorach took a man of the chessmen and made a cast at one of the ravens that struck his beak and his throat, and Fermaise killed the second, and Caoilte the third.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Elcmar's daughter made a bed of healing for Caoilte, and a bowl of pale gold was brought to her full of water, and she bruised herbs into it, and he took five drinks of it that made him cast up the poison of the spear; and the washing of Flann, daughter of Flidais, was done for his head, that will never be troubled with pain, or baldness, or weakness of sight. And the people of the hill gave good gifts to Caoilte — a fish-hook that was called Aicil mac Mogha, that could not be set in any river or inver but it would take fish, and along with that a drink of remembrance, and after that drink there would be no place he ever saw, or no battle or fight he ever was in, but it would stay in his memory.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VII; not verbatim.
